messages.subject: Differential functioning of items and test for the GGUM
messages.subject_clean: Differential functioning of items and test for the GGUM
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm curious if anyone in this group has any reproducible materials they can share regarding how to use the mirt package to conduct an assessment of differential functioning of items and tests, specifically using the generalized graded unfolding model (GGUM).

Thanks in advance. – Chris

messages.subject: Re: Differential functioning of items and test for the GGUM
messages.subject_clean: Differential functioning of items and test for the GGUM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I have very negative feelings about the DFIT framework for this purpose, and have written about a better alternative in the paper here: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-018-9626-9 For now I'd recommend using the DRF() function in mirt to obtain these types of statistics but avoids all the negative aspects of the DFIT approach. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Interpretation of IRT model formulas on 'package mirt’ documentation
messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of IRT model formulas on 'package mirt’ documentation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Sorry if this is a very basic question. Could I ask how to interpret the IRT formulas presented on p.99 of the 'Package mirt' documentation (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mirt/mirt.pdf)? To focus on one, below is the 4pl formula provided:

As I understand it:

 - P gives the probability
 - x=1 refers to 1 person
 - theta represents ability
 - g represents guessing
 - u represents fatigue
 - a represents the item level coefficient
 - d represents the group level coefficient
 - exp denotes employment of the exponential function

I think the above is correct, but please let me know if not!

However, I have seen the symbol ψ used in various ways in IRT literature. E.g., the "collection of all item parameters" (Chalmers, 2012) and variance of the factor (MPlus guidance). Otherwise, this symbol might typically refer to the functional form (i.e., logistic).

How should I interpret the ψ symbol in the above 4pl formula?

Also, what do subscript 1 and subscript 2 denote in this formula?

Thanks very much in advance and apologies for my lack of general understanding,

Joe

messages.body_plain:
When you say 'prior item parameters' are you referring to applying Bayesian prior distributions, or starting values. If the latter, here's an example that changes the starting values of the model using the usual pars = 'values' chain. In this example, the model also converges instantly due to the TOL = NA argument.

http://philchalmers.github.io/SimDesign/html/04-Auxillary_parameter_recovery.html

Phil

>
> As I understand it:
>
>  - P gives the probability
>  - x=1 refers to 1 person

A response of x=1 for a single person.

>  - theta represents ability
>  - g represents guessing
>  - u represents fatigue

This is usually called carelessness

>  - a represents the item level coefficient

slope/discrimination

>  - d represents the group level coefficient

easiness of item

>  - exp denotes employment of the exponential function

I just use that as a collection vector. It just represents a vector of arbitrary length to collect relevant parameters. So in the above equation phi = [a1, a2, d, g, u], provided all of those are estimated.

>
> How should I interpret the ψ symbol in the above 4pl formula?
>
> Also, what do subscript 1 and subscript 2 denote in this formula?

The respective dimensions. If you want to get a feel for this model try the interactive template via

> itemplot(shiny=TRUE)

Phil

messages.subject_clean: [mirtCAT] Insert plot on the last page
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jungmin,

The key is the lastpage function though you are correct this is a little different. The plot(results) output happens after the mirtCAT() function exits, and contains a lot more information than needed to make a plot. You'll have to use the information in the person object in lastpage(person) to draw the type of graphic you want and return the information in the list() output. I can try to make an example of this if it would be helpful.

Phil

To get p-values in mirt you'll have to divide the parameter estimates from coef(mod, printSE=TRUE) by their associated SE, and use the 2 * pnorm(p/SE, lower.tail=FALSE) approach to get the two-tailed large sample p-value.

Phil

messages.subject: DIF and DTF
messages.subject_clean: DIF and DTF
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I'm attempting to look at DIF and DTF between two groups on a scale from a very large data set (over 80k). I'm trying to follow the process in your 2016 paper (It Might Not Make a Big DIF...). Essentially, I'm wondering if I'm going about the approach correctly.

In this case, I don't have any a priori sense of which item(s) will exhibit DIF, so first I ran an unconstrained reference model just to see if any items were evidencing DIF (and/or latent trait distribution differences):

> mod_PHQref <- multipleGroup(PHQresp, 1, PHQ_SGMid, SE = TRUE,
>                               technical = list(removeEmptyRows = TRUE, NCYCLES = 1000))
> mod_PHQ_DIF0 <- DIF(mod_PHQref, c("a1", "d"), plotdif = TRUE)

Items 1, 2, 4, and 8 looked to potentially exhibit DIF (there's also pretty good evidence of uniform DIF from the plot attached), so I then fit a constrained model using the other items as anchors, and ran a DIF analysis specifying the suspected DIF items to test:

> mod_PHQ1 <- multipleGroup(PHQresp, 1, PHQ_SGMid, SE = TRUE,
>                               invariance=c(PHQ_SGMitems[c(3,5:7,9)], 'free_means', 'free_var'),
>                               technical = list(removeEmptyRows = TRUE, NCYCLES = 1000))
> mod_PHQ_DIF1 <- DIF(mod_PHQ1, c("a1", "d"), items2test = c(1:2,4,8))

>From the output, it now looks like only two of the items are significant (after equating?), but I'm not sure if I'm interpreting it correctly.

>                    AIC         AICc     SABIC        HQ        BIC         X2  df           p
> phq9_1      1.539      1.541      7.582     4.374   10.760     0.461   1   0.497
> phq9_2     -3.984     -3.981      2.060    -1.149     5.238    5.984    1  0.014
> phq9_4     -1.310     -1.307      4.734     1.526     7.912    3.310    1  0.069
> phq9_8   -52.162   -52.159   -46.118 - 49.326  -42.940  54.162    1  0.000

Finally, I estimated DTF with 1000 draws:

> $observed
>    sDTF.score.    sDTF(%).score    uDTF.score      uDTF(%).score
>    0.09468049    0.26300137         0.09468049      0.26300137
>
> $CIs
>               sDTF.score     sDTF(%).score     uDTF.score      uDTF(%).score
> CI_97.5 0.11746785            0.3262996     0.11746785      0.3262996
> CI_2.5   0.07185844            0.1996068     0.07185844     0.1996068
>
> $tests
> P(sDTF.score = 0)
>      1.722971e-16

So, I would interpret this as significant sDTF statistic but with relatively small effect size. It seems strange here that the sDTF and uDTF scores are the same (this is a red flag to me that I'm doing something wrong). I also tried the above but using the drop_sequential approach rather than specifying items using items2test. I got 8 errors here that say "M-step optimizer converged immediately. Solution is either at the ML or starting values are causing issues and should be adjusted." So, I'm not sure what's going on there.

In any case, any guidance you could give me would be appreciated!

Nicholas

messages.subject_clean: Formative model replacement with facet constructs and single reflective measures
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rico,

While this isn't possible in mirt, you probably could have some luck if you combined some of the output from mirt with other software like lavaan. After you fit your measurement model what you can do is invoke plausible value imputations via the fscores() function to obtain quasi-plausible draws for each latent trait score (with the stochastic variability included in each draw), and use these as observed scores to be input into lavaan to form the formative measure in the reset of the diagram. You'd have to repeat this a number of times and average over the results though (including the between-within sampling variability as well in the SE computations), but that should give a reasonable representation of the phenomenon at hand. Or, if it happens that your observed items are all 2PL/graded response models then working in the SEM framework entirely would be sufficient. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: DIF and DTF
messages.subject_clean: DIF and DTF
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicholas,

Your approach sounds pretty good to me, though these days I would recommend using the DRF() function rather than DTF() (there's an associated paper explaining why which is reference in the help file). The setup is basically the same, but DRF has a better interpretation as an effect size to be interpreted, while DTF() is largely good for detecting DTF but not necessarily quantifying its overall impact. Also, sDTF and uDTF can be exactly the same when the response curves never cross, which is more of a feature than a cause for concern. This basically means that no compensatory effects were observed, so interpreting either statistic is fine (same goes for the DRF family). HTH.

Phil

P.S. From the output, only phq9_8 probably shows DIF after controlling for family-wise error.

Den torsdag 25 juli 2019 kl. 05:44:23 UTC+2 skrev Phil Chalmers:

> Hi Rico,
>
> While this isn't possible in mirt, you probably could have some luck if you combined some of the output from mirt with other software like lavaan. After you fit your measurement model what you can do is invoke plausible value imputations via the fscores() function to obtain quasi-plausible draws for each latent trait score (with the stochastic variability included in each draw), and use these as observed scores to be input into lavaan to form the formative measure in the reset of the diagram. You'd have to repeat this a number of times and average over the results though (including the between-within sampling variability as well in the SE computations), but that should give a reasonable representation of the phenomenon at hand. Or, if it happens that your observed items are all 2PL/graded response models then working in the SEM framework entirely would be sufficient. HTH.
>
> Phil
